chunks.section: Delayed Effects of Temporary Weight Decay in Muon Pretraining

A temporary optimization intervention can increase validation loss when it ends yet reduce it at the final training budget. We demonstrate this with temporary weight decay in Muon-trained decoder-only Transformers with 162M, 405M, 1.4B, and 3.4B parameters. For models up to 1.4B parameters, moving a fixed-duration decay window from early to late training reverses its final effect. At 162M, changing window duration alters final loss even at approximately matched total shrinkage. Most strikingly, a schedule selected at 162M and transferred without retuning to 1.4B is 0.26 nats worse than no decay when removed, overtakes it only after 73% of training, and ultimately finishes 0.028 nats better while also outperforming the best sampled constant-decay baseline. Early decay leaves a persistent weight-norm deficit, which keeps relative steps larger after the intervention ends. An approximate norm-dynamics recurrence captures the slow convergence of these relative steps, and fixed-norm replays of the measured trajectories reproduce the performance ordering and a similar loss difference. At 162M and 405M, norm-reset experiments show that smaller weight norms at the end of the decay window explain most of the final loss improvement. A separate Gram intervention exhibits related post-removal norm and relative-step dynamics. These results show that temporary optimization schedules can have delayed effects long after removal and should therefore be evaluated at the intended final training budget, not only at removal. † † date: November 12, 2026 † † correspondence: Md Rifat Arefin at rifat.arefin@mila.quebec

A temporary optimization intervention can increase validation loss when it ends and reduce it much later, even after the intervention has been removed. Figure 1 shows an extreme example. In a 1.4B-parameter Transformer ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) trained with Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , a temporary weight-decay schedule leaves validation loss 0.26 0.26 nats worse than no decay when the schedule ends. Both runs then continue with the same explicit update rule. Nevertheless, the treated run gradually recovers, overtakes the no-decay baseline only after 73 % \% of training, and finishes 0.0275 0.0275 nats better. Performance at the endpoint of an intervention can therefore be a poor predictor of its eventual effect.

Temporary changes during early training are known to have lasting effects on the learned solution ( Achille et al., 2017 ; Frankle et al., 2020 ) , and prior work has shown that regularization can matter disproportionately during early learning ( Golatkar et al., 2019 ) . We study a different aspect of this phenomenon: the effect of a temporary intervention can continue to evolve after the intervention has ended, to the point that its sign or ranking changes at later checkpoints. This creates a basic problem for evaluating temporary optimization schedules. Such schedules are usually specified by an update rule and the interval over which it is applied. But when the intervention ends, the treated and reference runs generally enter the subsequent phase with different parameters and optimizer states. Their loss difference can therefore continue to evolve even though their explicit update rules are again identical. Evaluating an intervention when it is removed can consequently select a schedule that is inferior at the intended final training budget—or reject one that will eventually be beneficial.

We study this phenomenon using temporary weight decay in Muon-trained decoder-only Transformers. Weight decay provides a particularly controlled setting: turning it off cleanly separates its direct shrinkage from the training state it leaves behind. Muon also provides a useful connection between weight norms and subsequent optimization. Its matrix updates have approximately controlled magnitude, so for a given projected update norm, reducing the weight norm increases the update size relative to the current weights ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Kosson et al., 2023 ; Wen et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Temporary decay can therefore alter subsequent optimization even after its coefficient has returned to zero. We ask two related questions: Central question. How should a temporary optimization intervention be evaluated, and what aspects of the training state carry its effect after the intervention is removed? We address the first question by varying when decay starts, how long it lasts, and when its effect is evaluated. Across models from 162M to 1.4B parameters, moving a fixed-duration decay window from early to late training reverses its final effect: early windows improve final loss, whereas a window beginning at 60 % 60\% of training hurts. At 405M, even among beneficial early schedules, the ranking changes depending on whether they are compared at a common final training budget or after the same amount of post-removal training. At 162M, changing window duration also changes final loss substantially even when total multiplicative shrinkage is approximately matched. These results separate three notions that are often conflated: when an intervention acts, how long the model trains after it is removed, and the final budget at which it is evaluated.

We address the second question by examining what remains different after decay is removed. Early decay leaves a persistent weight-norm deficit, which keeps relative steps larger than in the no-decay run long after both models resume the same update rule. An approximate recurrence accounts for the slow convergence of these relative-step trajectories. An opposite perturbation—boosting the learning rate early—raises weight norms and leaves relative steps smaller after the boost ends, as predicted by the same account. More directly, fixed-norm replays using the measured relative-step trajectories reproduce the performance ordering and a similar loss difference; swapping trajectories at the end of the decay window shows that most of the replay advantage arises from the altered steps after decay has ended. These experiments explain how an early intervention can continue to modify optimization after removal, although they do not establish that norms are the only persistent state or explain why a particular relative-step trajectory is beneficial. Together, these experiments characterize both the evaluation consequences of delayed optimization effects and one mechanism by which an early intervention can remain active through the state it leaves behind.

Temporary changes during early optimization can have lasting effects on the learned solution. Achille et al. (2017) and Frankle et al. (2020) study critical early phases in neural-network training, showing that perturbations applied near initialization can influence later optimization and the final solution. Most directly related, Golatkar et al. (2019) show in image classification that weight decay and data augmentation matter disproportionately during early learning and comparatively little near convergence. Our focus is different: we study what happens after a temporary intervention is removed. In our setting, the loss difference can continue to evolve for a large fraction of training, reverse sign, and change the ranking of schedules even though the treated and reference runs again use the same explicit update rule.

chunks.section: Weight norms and effective step size.
chunks.text: Several recent works characterize the relation between weight decay, parameter norms, and effective learning rate. Kosson et al. (2023) analyze rotational equilibrium under weight decay; Wen et al. (2026) derive related equilibrium behavior for Muon and introduce Hyperball, which controls weight and update norms; Liu et al. (2026) connect effective learning rate to language-model loss dynamics; Kosson et al. (2024) analyze the large relative steps produced by weights below equilibrium. These works characterize persistent coefficients, equilibrium behavior, or explicit norm control. We instead study the transient after temporary decay is removed: the weights can remain far below the no-decay norm trajectory, causing relative step sizes to remain different long after both runs resume the same explicit update rule.

Recent work has characterized Muon through spectral-norm constraints and row-norm control ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Lion et al., 2026 ) . Our experiments are complementary: rather than modifying Muon’s norm control directly, we ask how an earlier temporary intervention changes the optimization trajectory that Muon follows afterward. The resulting norm deficit provides a concrete state variable through which the effect of a removed intervention can persist.

We train decoder-only Transformers with 162M, 405M, 1.4B, and 3.4B parameters. The main configuration uses Muon, a matrix optimizer that orthogonalizes momentum updates, with squared-ReLU ( ReLU 2 \mathrm{ReLU}^{2} ) MLPs, a context length of 1,024, and 1,024 sequences per update. The learning rate is 0.01 for the first 90% of training and decreases linearly to zero over the final 10%. The default configuration has no initial warmup; Section 6.3 tests 10% linear warmup and shows that the delayed crossover persists. The compute-optimal budget is about 20 tokens per parameter ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . Matched intervention and reference runs share initialization, data order, and learning-rate schedule. Main timing and scale experiments use FineWeb100B, a 100B-token sample of FineWeb, while the replicated mechanism experiments use FineWeb-Edu ( Penedo et al., 2024 ) . Table 2 in Appendix A gives the dataset and reference for each experiment group. Losses are compared only within matched groups.

For each hidden-layer weight matrix, decoupled weight decay ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017 ) gives W t + 1 = ( 1 − η t λ t ) W t − η t U t , λ t = λ 𝟏 { s ≤ t < e } , W_{t+1}=(1-\eta_{t}\lambda_{t})W_{t}-\eta_{t}U_{t},\qquad\lambda_{t}=\lambda\mathbf{1}_{\{s\leq t<e\}}, (1) where U t U_{t} is the Muon update before multiplication by the learning rate η t \eta_{t} , and [ s , e ) [s,e) is the intervention window. Decay is zero outside this window unless a constant background coefficient is stated. Embeddings and the output head receive no decay.

All losses are next-token cross-entropy on held-out validation tokens, in nats per token (Appendix A ). We report Δ t = ℒ intervention ​ ( t ) − ℒ reference ​ ( t ) \Delta_{t}=\mathcal{L}_{\rm intervention}(t)-\mathcal{L}_{\rm reference}(t) at update t t ; the final difference is Δ T \Delta_{T} at the last update T T , and negative values indicate an improvement. We call the end of the window removal . In the timing experiments, early windows start within the first 20% of training and the late window starts at 60%. The best sampled constant is the best of the constant coefficients we tried for that scale and training setting, and the best reference is the better of this baseline and no decay. In the main timing and scale comparisons, claims that a schedule helps are made against both. Other experiment groups use the references specified in Appendix A . We use no decay alone when asking what the window itself changes (Section 5 ), because constant decay adds norm dynamics of its own.

Having established the delayed crossover in Figure 1 , we now separate three properties of a temporary schedule: when the window starts, how long it lasts, and when its effect is evaluated. These factors need not agree in their ranking of schedules because they determine both the state at removal and the subsequent optimization trajectory.

chunks.section: 4.1 A Short Early Window Improves Final Loss
chunks.text: We first verify the effect in a replicated comparison. Across five paired 162M runs, a 320-update early-decay window improves final loss by 0.0172 nats over no decay and by 0.0074 nats over the best sampled constant (Appendix C , Table 5 ).

chunks.section: 4.2 Start Time Changes the Sign; Evaluation Time Changes the Ranking
chunks.text: At all three scales, a 10% window starting at initialization beats both references, whereas the same-duration, same-coefficient window starting at 60% is worse than both (Figure 2 (a); Appendix C ). Within each scale these windows lie in the constant-learning-rate phase and apply the same multiplicative shrinkage, so the sign reversal is a timing effect rather than a difference in total shrinkage. Figure 2: Start time changes the sign; evaluation horizon changes the ranking. (a) Final loss difference for 10% windows by start time; dashed lines show the best sampled constant. (b) At 405M, the ranking of early starts reverses when evaluated after equal post-removal training. Comparing at the final checkpoint fixes total training, whereas comparing a fixed number of updates after removal fixes post-removal training. At 405M these two evaluations reverse the ranking of the early schedules (Figure 2 (b)): the 20 % 20\% -start window is better at the common final checkpoint, while the initialization-start window is better after equal post-removal training. For the 0 % 0\% and 20 % 20\% starts, the equal-continuation checkpoints remain in the constant-learning-rate phase, so the reversal is not caused by the final learning-rate decay; the 60 % 60\% start is less directly comparable because its continuation enters that phase. Thus, the preferred early start depends on the evaluation horizon, although early starts help and the late start hurts under both comparisons.

chunks.section: 4.3 Duration Changes Outcomes beyond Total Shrinkage
chunks.text: Across our grid, final loss is more sensitive to window duration than to the decay coefficient. At fixed coefficient, varying duration changes the final improvement by 0.026–0.035 nats; at fixed duration, varying the coefficient changes it by only 0.007–0.010 nats. We train 162M models for 16,000 updates, five times the compute-optimal budget, in a 4 × 3 4\times 3 grid of durations and coefficients, with every window starting at initialization. At each coefficient, longer windows give lower loss (Figure 3 (a)). The best sampled constant, 0.05 0.05 , improves on no decay by 0.0122. Ten of the twelve cells beat it; the two that do not are the shortest windows with the two smallest coefficients. To separate the two effects, we compare schedules with approximately equal total log-shrinkage, D = − ∑ t log ( 1 − η t λ t ) . D=-\sum_{t}\log(1-\eta_{t}\lambda_{t}). (2) For three schedules with D ≈ 2.1 D\approx 2.1 , the magnitude of the final improvement more than doubles as the window lengthens from 700 to 3,564 updates (Figure 3 (b)). Matching D D fixes how much the initial weights are scaled down, but not how later updates are scaled (Appendix E ).

chunks.section: 4.3 Duration Changes Outcomes beyond Total Shrinkage
chunks.text: The best schedule in this grid, λ = 0.15 \lambda=0.15 over the first 44% of training, improves on the best sampled constant by 0.0335. We select this schedule here, at 162M, and transfer it without retuning to the 1.4B experiment in Figure 1 and Section 6.1 . It is also the longest window in this grid, so these runs do not locate the optimal duration. Separate fixed-coefficient sweeps at the compute-optimal budget find an interior optimum at both 162M and 405M, beyond which longer windows hurt (Appendix C ). Together, these experiments show that a temporary schedule cannot be ranked from its removal-time loss or total shrinkage alone. Start time, duration, and evaluation horizon can all change the comparison, because they alter either the state at removal or the amount of subsequent optimization. We next ask which component of that state can preserve the effect of an earlier decay window.

chunks.section: 5 A Persistent Norm Deficit Changes Later Relative Steps
chunks.text: Once decay is removed, the explicit update rule is again the same as in the no-decay run. Any continuing effect must therefore be carried by the parameters or optimizer state created during the intervention. Temporary decay can change weight directions, weight norms, and momentum. We focus on norms because they directly affect the size of a Muon update relative to the current weights. We first show that early decay leaves a long-lived norm deficit and correspondingly larger relative steps; we then test the relative-step trajectory directly with fixed-norm replays, before analyzing why the difference converges only slowly. This analysis explains how an early intervention can continue to modify optimization after removal, but does not establish that norms are the only persistent state or explain why a particular relative-step trajectory lowers loss.

chunks.section: 5.3 Replaying the relative-step trajectory reproduces the gain
chunks.text: Figure 5: Fixed-norm replay reproduces the post-removal gain. 162M, FineWeb-Edu, 3,200 updates. (a) Relative-step trajectories measured from the source Muon runs and replayed at fixed weight norms. (b) Final loss relative to Muon without decay; dots show three replay seeds and the last two bars switch trajectory at update 320. The correlation between smaller norms and larger relative steps does not establish that the altered relative-step trajectory matters for loss. To test this directly, we remove norm variation altogether. Using a variant of Hyperball ( Wen et al., 2026 ) , we hold every weight norm at its initial value and prescribe the relative-step trajectory α t \alpha_{t} measured from either the no-decay or early-decay Muon run, averaged over the six matrix families (Figure 5 (a)). Across three replay seeds, the trajectory measured from the early-decay run improves final loss by 0.022 to 0.023 nats relative to the no-decay trajectory, compared with a 0.0171-nat difference between the Muon runs from which the trajectories were taken (Figure 5 (b)). Thus, with norms fixed, the measured relative-step trajectories reproduce both the ordering and a similar magnitude of the original loss difference. A trajectory-swap experiment localizes where this difference arises. Using no-decay steps during the first 320 updates and early-decay steps afterward accounts for 0.0181 of the 0.0221-nat replay difference. Conversely, replaying only the early-decay trajectory during the intervention and then returning to ordinary Muon improves loss by only 0.0003 nats. Most of the replay advantage therefore comes from the altered relative steps after weight decay has already been removed (Figure 5 (b)).

chunks.section: 5.3 Replaying the relative-step trajectory reproduces the gain
chunks.text: The replay uses a modified optimizer and averages α t \alpha_{t} over matrix families, so it does not show that relative steps are the only relevant state. It does show that the observed post-removal relative-step trajectory is sufficient, in this controlled setting, to reproduce the performance ordering and approximate loss difference. Resetting block norms at removal removes or recovers most of the early-decay advantage at 162M and 405M (Appendix H ).

chunks.section: 5.4 Why do the trajectories converge so slowly?
chunks.text: The early learning-rate boosts introduced in Section 5.2 provide an opposite-sign check of this account: they raise the norms and produce persistent reductions in later relative steps, with the measured offsets behaving as predicted by the same recurrence (Appendix G ). At 1.4B, we do not have the corresponding relative-step logs for the no-decay run, so we cannot test the recurrence as directly. We can nevertheless track the norm deficit itself. From update 14,000 to 25,200, the layer-averaged squared-norm gap between the no-decay and early-decay runs grows by 39 % 39\% for W V W_{V} and W O W_{O} and 17 % 17\% for W down W_{\mathrm{down}} while the squared norms in the no-decay run roughly double. Thus, the absolute deficit does not remain fixed, but it becomes progressively smaller relative to the growing weight norms, consistent with the slow recovery seen at 162M.

The norm account explains why an early intervention can continue to alter optimization after removal, but not which relative-step trajectory is beneficial. Larger relative steps are not universally better. Continuing with decay coefficient 0.10 0.10 after the window keeps relative steps larger than stopping decay, yet yields a smaller final improvement (0.0071 versus 0.0171 nats; Figure 4 (b)). Likewise, a window starting at 60% of training shrinks the weights by the same factor as one starting at initialization but hurts final loss (Figure 2 (a)). Thus, persistent norm and relative-step differences explain the delayed influence of the intervention, not why early and late trajectories have opposite effects.

We next test whether the delayed effect persists across model scale and training conditions. We first transfer a schedule selected at 162M directly to 1.4B without retuning, then compare shorter windows across scale and test robustness to longer training, warmup, architecture, and optimizer choice.

chunks.section: 6.1 A schedule selected at 162M transfers to 1.4B
chunks.text: We transfer the best schedule from the 162M duration sweep— λ = 0.15 \lambda=0.15 for the first 44 % 44\% of training—to a 1.4B model without retuning. It finishes 0.0275 nats ahead of no decay and 0.0264 ahead of the best sampled constant-decay baseline; as Figure 1 shows, this advantage emerges entirely after removal. The best schedule sampled directly at 1.4B improves on the transferred schedule by only 0.0020 0.0020 nats.

A 10% decay window starting at initialization beats both no decay and the best sampled constant at every scale (Table 1 ). At 405M, the first-10% window improves over no decay by 0.0247 0.0247 – 0.0262 0.0262 nats across three matched seeds, and over constant 0.02 0.02 by 0.0172 0.0172 – 0.0194 0.0194 nats. More broadly, every tested constant coefficient improves on no decay at 162M and 405M, whereas at 1.4B only the two smallest tested coefficients do so, and only slightly. These comparisons show that the benefit of an early window persists across the tested scales, but not that its magnitude follows a scaling law: the fixed 10 % 10\% schedule is also farther from the best sampled duration at 162M than at the larger scales. The effect is not limited to the compute-optimal, no-warmup configuration. At 162M trained for 64,000 updates— 20 × 20\times the compute-optimal budget—a first-10% window still beats the best sampled constant by 0.0180 nats (Appendix C ). With 10% linear warmup, a decay window confined to warmup ties the best sampled constant at 162M and beats it at 405M and 1.4B; extending decay beyond warmup restores a clear advantage at 162M and 405M. Importantly, warmup does not eliminate the delayed crossover: in a 16,000-update 162M run, temporary decay is 0.0237 nats worse than no decay at update 8,000 but 0.0373 nats better by update 14,400 (Appendix F ). Early decay also improves loss with SwiGLU MLPs and with AdamW at 162M, but not with AdamW at 405M (Appendix C ). Thus, the phenomenon is robust to several training variations but is not optimizer-independent. Across four data domains, temporary decay improves on constant 0.01 0.01 both at removal and at the final checkpoint, but the domain ranking changes between the two evaluations; Appendix D reports these comparisons and exploratory corpus-level analyses.

chunks.section: 7 A Second Norm-Changing Intervention Shows Related Dynamics
chunks.text: The preceding mechanism could be specific to the multiplicative form of weight decay. We therefore test a qualitatively different intervention that also changes weight norms. During an early window, we add the off-diagonal Gram penalty ℛ t = μ 𝟏 { 0 ≤ t < e } ∑ ℓ = 1 L ∑ W ∈ { W V , W O , W down } E ( W ℓ ) , E ( W ) = ∥ OffDiag ( W ⊤ W ) ∥ F 2 . \mathcal{R}_{t}=\mu\mathbf{1}_{\{0\leq t<e\}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\sum_{W\in\{W_{V},W_{O},W_{\mathrm{down}}\}}E(W_{\ell}),\qquad E(W)=\|\OffDiag(W^{\top}W)\|_{F}^{2}. (5) Muon orthogonalizes the combined task and penalty gradient, so the applied update is not the raw penalty gradient (Appendix A ). The Gram penalty exhibits the same qualitative timing dependence as temporary decay. At 162M, 10% windows starting at 0%, 20%, and 60% of training change final loss by -0.0147, -0.0080, and +0.0209 nats, respectively. Across five paired 162M runs, an early Gram penalty improves final loss by 0.0142 nats relative to no regularization. The raw penalty gradient contains a radial component that changes the weight norm and a tangential component that changes only direction to first order. Radial–tangential and state-copy controls indicate that norm changes account for much of the improvement: when applied after the Muon update, the radial component nearly matches the full penalty while the tangential component has little effect, and copying column norms recovers more of the advantage than copying normalized column correlations (Appendix E ). The penalty also leaves larger post-removal relative steps primarily in the matrices it targets (Appendix G ). Early Gram regularization also improves loss at 162M and 405M across both tested datasets, while 1.4B requires retuning of its strength (Appendix B ).

chunks.section: 7 A Second Norm-Changing Intervention Shows Related Dynamics
chunks.text: Together, these results provide evidence that the post-removal norm and relative-step dynamics of Section 5 are not unique to multiplicative weight decay, without implying that norm reduction is generally beneficial.

The endpoint of a temporary optimization intervention need not be the endpoint of its effect. In Muon pretraining, temporary decay can be worse at removal yet better at the final budget; both the sign and ranking of schedules can change after removal. This behavior persists across the tested scales, and a schedule selected at 162M transfers without retuning to 1.4B. Our mechanism experiments identify one way this delayed effect can be carried after removal. Early decay leaves a persistent weight-norm deficit and correspondingly larger relative steps; an approximate recurrence explains their slow convergence, and fixed-norm replays show that the measured relative-step trajectory is sufficient to reproduce the performance ordering and a similar loss difference. A separate Gram intervention exhibits related timing, norm, and post-removal relative-step behavior. These results explain how an early intervention can continue to alter optimization after it is removed, but not why a particular relative-step trajectory is beneficial: larger relative steps are not universally better, and we do not establish that norms are the only persistent state.

The practical implication is methodological: temporary schedules should be evaluated at the training budget at which the model will be used, not only when the intervention ends. Our conclusions are specific to the tested regimes. Most configurations outside the replicated comparisons use a single seed (Appendix A ). The numerical decay coefficients are not universal; detailed mechanism measurements are concentrated at 162M; some robustness comparisons use constant 0.01 0.01 rather than a full constant-decay sweep; and early decay does not improve every tested optimizer setting. Finally, the downstream evaluations at 405M and 1.4B do not show a clear advantage over constant decay; at 3.4B, early decay improves mean zero-shot accuracy over all tested references (Appendix K ). Whether similar delayed dynamics arise broadly across optimizers and temporary interventions remains an open question.

chunks.section: Replaying relative steps at fixed norm.
chunks.text: To isolate the relative-step trajectory, we remove norm changes. After each Muon step, a variant of Hyperball ( Wen et al., 2026 ) rescales the weight change of each matrix to Frobenius norm η t ​ ‖ W 0 ‖ F \eta_{t}\|W_{0}\|_{F} and projects the weights back to norm ‖ W 0 ‖ F \|W_{0}\|_{F} . Weight norms then stay at their initial values, and η t \eta_{t} sets the relative step. We prescribe the relative step using the six-family mean of the logged α t \alpha_{t} in either the no-decay run or the λ = 0.3 \lambda=0.3 run, interpolated linearly between logged updates (Figure 5 a). The replays use 162M, FineWeb-Edu, 3,200 updates, and no weight decay. Both trajectories come from seed 1234 and are reused for all three replay seeds. The early-decay trajectory beats the no-decay trajectory by 0.0221–0.0233 nats across the three replays, compared with 0.0171 nats between the Muon source runs (Figure 5 b). Splitting the trajectories at update 320 attributes 0.0181 nats of the 0.0221-nat replay difference to the post-window steps. Replaying only the early-window trajectory before continuing with ordinary Muon changes final loss by just 0.0003 nats. With norms held fixed, the early-decay trajectory reproduces the ordering and approximate size of the gain, and most of the replay gain comes from the larger relative steps after the window. Figure 8 relates these larger steps to the reduced norms.

chunks.text: The Gram runs also log α t \alpha_{t} . We divide α t \alpha_{t} in each Gram run by α t \alpha_{t} in a reference with the same background decay and no penalty. Immediately after removal, the targeted families take 1.3–2.7 times the reference relative step; near the end of training, the ratio is 1.04–1.11. After removal, untargeted families stay within 5% of the reference when W V W_{V} , W O W_{O} , and W down W_{\mathrm{down}} are all targeted. When only W down W_{\mathrm{down}} is targeted (SwiGLU), W V W_{V} and W up W_{\mathrm{up}} differ from the reference by up to 10% until about update 1,600. The Gram penalty therefore produces the same qualitative pattern as early decay—smaller norms and larger later relative steps—mainly in the matrices it targets.
